extracted.intended_audience: theologians, seminary students, and scholars of Catholic systematic theology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing competing theological systems of divine grace (Thomism, Molinism, Augustinianism, Congruism, Syncretism) with respect to doctrine, logical coherence, moral responsibility, and pastoral/psychological plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of true free-will (no praemotio ad unum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system must not make the will inevitably predetermined by God (a _praedeterminatio ad unum_) so that it can no longer be called truly free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text repeatedly objects that an efficacious physical premotion which 'predetermines the will' destroys freedom. The page stresses that liberty resides formally in the will (not merely in the intellect) and that any claimed faculty to resist (potentia dissentiendi/potentia resistendi) must be a real, activatable power, not a chimera (compare the man tied to a chair example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with Council definitions (Trent, Vatican)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of grace must accord with Magisterial decrees that a man can reject inspiration/effect of grace and that man 'coöperates by assenting' and can 'resist' grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from Trent and Vatican are used as definitive tests: e.g., Trent's anathemas and Vatican's definition that faith is a gift and 'the act of faith... is a work... by assenting to and coöperating with His grace, which he is able to resist.' Any system denying this is judged heretical or untenable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of making God the author of sin
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory system must not logically imply that God is the immediate author or cause of sinful acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomistic premises are criticized for implying God's predetermination of sinful acts (praemotio ad malum), which would make God author of sin; the text cites Trent's anathema against such views. The page insists on distinctions (actus vs malitia) and on mechanisms by which God can know sin without being its author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of divine foreknowledge (scientia media)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system must provide a plausible account of how God infallibly foreknows future free acts (including hypotheticals), e.g., via the Molinist _scientia media_.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Molinism's _scientia media_ is presented as a working hypothesis that explains how God knows 'futuribilia' (what a will would do if given grace) and thus can bestow efficacious graces with infallible success. The absence of such an account is treated as a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definition/distinction of sufficient vs efficacious grace
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must define how 'gratia sufficiens' differs from 'gratia efficax' and explain whether they differ intrinsically or by effect/ circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lays out competing accounts: Thomists (intrinsic difference _ab intrinseco_), Molinists (extrinsic/accidental distinction; sufficiency becomes efficacy by will), Augustinians (delectatio-based account). Critiques point out confusions (e.g., 'gratia parva' vs 'gratia magna') and require precise use of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of modus operandi of grace (threefold efficacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory account should explain how grace operates in terms of efficacy of power (virtutis), efficacy of union (connexionis), and efficacy of infallible success (infallibilitatis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congruism's threefold schema is presented: grace has its own virtus; the union between act and grace depends on free-will; infallible success is grounded in God's certain foreknowledge. A rubric asks for such a clear mechanism or equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical coherence and avoidance of evasive distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The system must avoid internal contradictions and cannot rely on subtle scholastic distinctions or appeals to omnipotence to mask a real contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rejects Thomist moves that distinguish 'necessitas consequentis' vs 'necessitas consequentiae' as evasive. Appeals to God's omnipotence cannot turn an intrinsic contradiction into a real possibility (analogy: cannot make a square circle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of moral responsibility (libertas a coactione and libertas a necessitate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must safeguard that the will is not coerced (libertas a coactione) and retains capacity to resist (libertas a necessitate as appropriate), so moral responsibility is meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Augustinians claim moral predetermination (praemotio moralis) leaves will free; the critique demands genuine capacity to resist at all times. If efficacious grace removes that capacity, the will's freedom (and moral responsibility) is compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real and operative power to dissent/resist (potentia dissentiendi)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theory asserts the will can dissent or resist under grace, that faculty must be genuinely operative; it must not be a merely nominal or logically inert 'potentia'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Thomist claim of a retained 'potentia dissentiendi' is judged inadequate if it can never be activated — compared to a tied man whose 'potentia standi' is neutralized. The rubric requires that claimed faculties have demonstrable efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct account of the relation between intellect and will (indifferentia iudicii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorizing must recognize that freedom 'formaliter' resides in the will, not solely in the intellect's indifferent representations; the intellect's presentation of an object as indifferent does not guarantee the will's freedom if external premotion compels the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes Thomist defenses that locate freedom in the intellect (indifferentia iudicii) rather than in the will, noting that formal freedom requires the will's internal ability to act or not act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with Scriptural and Patristic sources (esp. Augustine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should be defensible from Scripture and the Fathers, and must not misappropriate Augustine's language to support contradictory systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that Augustine's writings have been used to support contradictory systems and that faithful appeal to Augustine requires careful interpretation (criticizing 'Augustinus Iprensis' vs 'Augustinus Hipponensis').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible psychological/anthropological grounding (motives beyond delectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system must allow for a plurality of motives (fear, hatred, sorrow, duty) as causes of supernaturally good deeds, not reduce all to 'delectatio' (pleasure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Augustinianism's claim that celestial delectation is the font of all supernaturally good deeds is criticized as implausible; doctrine should account for diverse human motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for unequal distribution of efficacious grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories must explain why efficacious grace is given more powerfully or effectively to some persons than others (inequality of distribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congruism appeals to God's adaptation of grace to circumstances ('gratia congrua' vs 'incongrua'), while the author notes the mystery remains. A credible theory should address this distribution without diminishing God's omnipotence or attributing arbitrariness to creatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for God's dignity and omnipotence
rubrics_metrics.description: While explaining efficacy and congruity, the theory must not depict God as slavishly adapting Himself to creaturely circumstances in a way that diminishes divine majesty or omnipotence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique of Congruism warns that saying God 'adjusts himself slavishly to all the circumstances' undermines His dignity; a balance between divine initiative and accommodation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of conversion and saintly experiences (empirical fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plausible account should explain sudden and dramatic conversions or changes of heart (whether by congruity, intrinsic efficaciousness, or other means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congruism is criticized for being unable fully to explain sudden saintly conversions observed historically (the author argues grace sometimes works regardless of 'congruity'). The rubric rewards theories that can account for such phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise use and hierarchy of terms (gratia parva vs magna; proxime/remote sufficiens)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must use technical terms unambiguously and in accord with classical usages (e.g., Augustine's distinctions between 'gratia parva' and 'gratia magna').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Augustinian confusions about 'gratia parva' being called 'sufficient' then labeled ineffective; a sound theory must clarify whether 'gratia parva' is remote sufficiency (prayer) or proximate sufficiency (effective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of co-operation between grace and will (cooperatur assentiendo)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system must coherently explain how the will co-operates with grace — not as mere passivity, but as an act of assent that contributes to justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent language ('cooperatur assentiendo') is invoked as normative: grace enables and disposes, while the will assents. Systems that render the will 'inanimate and merely passive' are anathematized in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between divine causality and human contingency (avoid deterministic fatalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should avoid deterministic implications (that God compels all acts) while still providing a basis for predestination/finality (e.g., final perseverance) coherent with doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Molinism is praised for reconciling infallibility of grace with free-will (via scientia media) and for explaining predestination without destroying contingency; the rubric values such balanced explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality and efficacy of prayer in the economy of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: A viable system should assign prayer an important (possibly indispensable) role in obtaining efficacious grace and in mediating between extrinsic/intrinsic graces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syncretism is commended for insisting that 'the present economy of grace is essentially and intrinsically an economy of prayer.' The rubric treats the explanatory role of prayer as a positive feature when well-argued.
